description: Three hives stand a little crooked along a beech hedge on low timber stands — sky blue, buttermilk yellow, faded rose — the grass worn to a bare muddy path in front of their entrances, a flat river stone weighting the lid of the middle box.

Four mismatched hives lean gently along a hawthorn hedge on low timber stands — cornflower blue, brick red, mint green, one plain unpainted timber — the hedge pressing close behind them, a spare super upended beside the last box and serving as a seat.

Three hives sit a little out of true along a clipped beech hedge — dusty ochre, pale lilac, sky blue — on squat timber stands with the grass worn away in front, a coil of old hose looped on a fence post at the near end.

Four hives stand in a cheerful crooked row along a hawthorn hedge — buttermilk yellow, seafoam green, brick red, faded rose — their stands mossy at the feet, a boot-scraper planted in the ground at the gap in the hedge beside them.

Three hives lean companionably along a thick beech hedge on low timber stands — cornflower blue, dusty ochre, mint green — the hedge woven tight behind them, a length of old net curtain tacked over a gap between the first two boxes.

Four mismatched hives stand a little crooked in a row along a hawthorn hedge — pale lilac, buttermilk yellow, sky blue, one plain unpainted board — the grass scuffed bare in front, a rain gauge mounted on the nearest stand post and filled to the brim with fallen petals.

Three hives sit on a grassy bank under a gnarled old apple tree — sky blue, faded rose, dusty ochre — the forage growing thick and tangled right up around their stands, bees threading through the stems below the lowest board.

Four hives are set on a sloping bank under two old pear trees — mint green, buttermilk yellow, brick red, cornflower blue — the grass and clover pressing around every stand leg, windfall fruit browning softly in the growth between them.

Three hives rest on a wildflower bank under a broad old plum tree — pale lilac, seafoam green, faded rose — their stands half-buried in tall forage, a bucket of wax scraps sitting in the sun beside the lowest hive going slowly soft.

Four hives perch on a sloped bank under a pair of old apple trees — dusty ochre, sky blue, buttermilk yellow, brick red — the flowering growth reaching their entrance boards, a cracked terracotta pot wedged at the bank's edge holding a bunch of tail feathers.

A thick old stone wall holds three domed straw skeps in arched alcoves cut right into it, ferns pressing from every joint, a stone slab lintel laid flat over each niche, a flat stone weighting the crown of the nearest skep.

A broad old stone wall carries four skeps in deep arched alcoves, ferns and moss filling the joints between the courses, a stone slab lintel over every niche, a coil of spare twine and a folded cloth resting on the wall's flat cap beside them.

A thick dressed-stone wall shelters three domed straw skeps in rounded alcoves, each under a stone slab lintel with ferns growing from the cracks, a spare super standing upended on the ground at the wall's foot as a rough worktable.

A small open-fronted timber bee house stands on short posts, its corrugated tin roof patched with a square of new sheet, three hives inside painted sky blue, mint green and faded rose, the back wall drilled with a grid of holes stuffed with bundles of cut reed and hollow stem.

A low timber bee house with a shingle roof shelters four hives — buttermilk yellow, cornflower blue, brick red, one plain unpainted timber — the back wall behind them packed with reed bundles and hollow stems in a dense grid, a boot-scraper set at the open entrance.

A small bee house of rough-sawn timber stands with its front open, a corrugated tin roof over three hives painted dusty ochre, pale lilac and seafoam green, the back wall bristling with cut stems and reed bundles, a length of old net curtain tacked over one open side against the wind.

The honey room holds a hand-cranked extractor bolted square to the floorboards, a settling tank on a timber stand beside it, and racks of drying frames stacked against the far wall; the window sill is crowded with filled glass jars, and the light coming through it lies in a broad band across the nearest boards.

Inside the honey shed a hand-cranked extractor stands bolted at the centre, shelves of filled glass jars lining the walls, a settling tank on a low stand in the corner; the open half-door frames a soft hazy view of the hives and hedge beyond, and the light from it falls across the bench edge and the nearest jars.

The little honey room clusters around a hand-cranked extractor and a settling tank on a stand, racks of frames drying above and shelves of wax-sealed jars below; the small square window holds a blurred view of the orchard outside, its sill lined with jars, and the light through it reaches the nearest floorboards in a pale spread.

Two sawn log hives stand upright lashed into the fork of a broad old oak, moss covering their crowns in a soft green layer, timber plugs fitted into their tops, a flat stone laid against the base of each log to keep them steady on their perch.

Two sawn log hives are stood on low stone plinths at the foot of an old ash tree, their bark crowns furred with moss, timber plugs sealed into the tops, a cracked terracotta pot beside the nearest plinth holding a small bunch of dried grasses and feathers.

Two hives are strapped onto the bed of a small two-wheeled cart parked at the edge of a clover field — sky blue and buttermilk yellow — chocks wedged under both wheels, bees moving steadily between the boxes and the flowers, a spare super resting flat on the cart boards between the two hives.

Two hives strapped onto a small wooden cart at a flowering field's edge — brick red and mint green — sit over chocked wheels, the cart boards worn pale, a coil of rope tied to the rail and a length of old net curtain tucked under one strap to pad the box corner.

Three hives are tucked into the corner of a small orchard, the long grass and windfall apples crowding around a low picket fence that encloses them — sky blue, faded rose, dusty ochre — a flat stone weighting the lid of the outermost box.

Three hives stand in an orchard corner behind a low woven hurdle fence — cornflower blue, pale lilac, buttermilk yellow — the grass long and full of windfall fruit, a spare super upended beside the fence and worn smooth on top from being sat on.

The honey room's long bench runs the length of one wall under a row of wax-sealed jars, an uncapping tray at its centre and a settling tank on a low stand at the end; the window above the bench holds a soft hazy view of the hives outside, and the light from it lies along the bench boards and the nearest jar lids.

A small shed given over to the honey work holds a hand-cranked extractor in the middle of the floor and stacked empty supers to the ceiling on one side; the open door is propped with a flat stone and frames a blurred glimpse of the hedge beyond, its light reaching in across the extractor's base.

The honey room keeps a rack of drying frames along one wall and a shelf of filled jars along the other, a cracked enamel basin of warm water on the bench between them; the small window's sill is crowded with more jars, and the light through it spreads pale across the floorboards below.

A tidy timber honey room holds a settling tank on a stand with a wide jar waiting beneath its tap, a coil of wire and a pair of pliers on the bench behind; through the half-open door the painted hives read soft and small outside, and the light off them falls across the tank's shoulder and the bench edge.
